titulo: The US-Iran War Is a Game of Chicken. And Brazil Is at the Table, Like It or Not.
resumo: I'll be direct: the February 28 bombing changed the geopolitical chessboard irreversibly. The decapitation of Ayatollah Khamenei and the succession by Mojtaba Khamenei under jihad rhetoric…
corpo:
I'll be direct: the February 28 bombing changed the geopolitical chessboard irreversibly. The decapitation of Ayatollah Khamenei and the succession by Mojtaba Khamenei under jihad rhetoric turned what was strategic tension into a war of national survival. This isn't a headline. It's a macroeconomic variable.

And most of the Brazilian market is still looking at IPCA as if it were a domestic problem.

It isn't. It's an exogenous shock with direct transmission.

I spend a good part of my time on risk models and stress scenarios. And what caught my attention in this crisis wasn't oil going up. That's obvious. What caught my attention was the structure of the game.

Anyone who's studied Thomas Schelling knows: what's happening between the US/Israel and Iran is a classic Game of Chicken. Two players accelerating toward each other. Whoever swerves first loses credibility. Whoever doesn't swerve might die.

The Nash Equilibrium here isn't peace. It's prolonged, high-intensity friction. And that changes everything for anyone pricing assets.

For Iran, swerving means losing regional hegemony and strategic relevance. For the US, swerving means admitting its security architecture in the Middle East is obsolete. Neither side can swerve without an unacceptable political cost. So the game continues.

And this is where the concept that interests me most as an engineer by training comes in: cost asymmetry.

An Iranian Shahed drone costs between US$30,000 and US$50,000. A Patriot interceptor costs US$4 million per shot. Iran is operating with negative convexity over the Western defense budget. Every cheap attack forces an expensive response. This isn't terrorism. It's economic engineering of attrition.

And the Strait of Hormuz, through which 21% of the world's oil transits, is the lever. It's the collateral.

Now let's get to what matters for anyone investing in Brazil.

The Treasury's Technical Note from March 2026 puts the numbers on the table. Comparing the February base scenario with the disruptive shock scenario (Brent at US$100):

Brent: from US$65.97 to US$100.00. A 51.5% increase.

GDP: from 2.30% to 2.66%. Up 0.36 p.p.

IPCA: from 3.60% to 4.28%. Up 0.68 p.p.

IGP-DI: from 4.60% to 4.90%.

Additional trade surplus: +US$10.3 billion.

Additional net tax revenue: +R$96.6 billion.

Read these numbers carefully.

Brazil gains R$96.6 billion in extra fiscal revenue with high oil prices. GDP rises. The trade surplus expands. Sounds great, right?

Not so fast.

IPCA goes to 4.28%, pressuring the ceiling of the target. IGP-DI jumps because of the extractive industry and nitrogen fertilizers. Household debt is already at 80.2%, which means any cost pass-through at the pump compresses real consumption. And capital flight toward US Treasuries pressures the exchange rate and risk premiums on our assets.

This is Brazil's dilemma: we're net oil exporters, but importers of stability. The commodity's appreciation enriches the State and impoverishes the household. It's an internal asymmetry that mirrors the asymmetry of the conflict abroad.

The government's response came via Provisional Measure (MP) 1,340/2026. There are three mechanisms:

A subsidy of R$0.32 per liter of road diesel, capped at R$10 billion. A 12% Export Tax on crude oil (NCM 2709). A 50% Export Tax on diesel (NCM 2710.19.21) for as long as the subsidy lasts.

In practice, the MP transfers part of the export surplus to contain the pass-through of the shock to domestic fuel prices. The direct target is diesel, which is the base cost of agricultural freight. The projected harvest of 344.1 million tons depends on viable shipping. If diesel rises without a cushion, the freight cost contaminates the agro-export chain and food inflation accelerates.

Penalties for abusive price increases across the distribution chain were recalibrated to a range of R$50,000 to R$500 million (Law No. 9,847/1999).

The net effect of the MP is still open. Its effectiveness depends on the duration of the conflict, distributor compliance, and exchange rate behavior. These are variables no model controls precisely at this moment.

But the central point I want to leave you with isn't about the crisis. It's about what comes next.

R$96.6 billion in additional fiscal revenue is a significant volume. The question that imposes itself is: where does that money go?

Brazil has known structural bottlenecks that this bonus could address or ignore:

First, refining and storage. The country is a net oil exporter, but remains exposed to derivatives market volatility due to insufficient refining capacity.

Second, nitrogen fertilizers. The 344 million ton harvest depends on imported inputs, some of them originating in the Middle East. Any prolonged disruption to Persian Gulf routes is a direct risk to agricultural productivity.

Third, logistical concentration. Dependence on chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz is a systemic vulnerability factor for any economy that depends on global trade.

Sérgio Botton Barcellos frames the issue precisely: national sovereignty in times of crisis is measured by the ability to combine control over energy vectors with long-term state policies. A country that exports raw commodities and imports derivatives remains vulnerable to the power cycles of major powers.

A State's ability to navigate asymmetric shocks without disintegrating its social fabric or its productive base is what will define positions in the new international order.

The US-Iran conflict isn't just a war. It's a stress test for every economic model that depends on global chains.

Brazil has a fiscal window opened by the shock. What's done with it will determine whether the country emerges from this crisis with more structural resilience or just a one-off surplus.

This is the kind of variable that doesn't show up in any model, but defines long-term trajectories.
